sources.claim: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Part 2: Copyrightability (January 29, 2025): given current generally available technology, prompts alone do not give enough human control to make the user the author of the output; human-authored expression, and human selection, arrangement or modification of AI output, can be protected.

sections.skill: Check the rights and terms that apply before using generated music

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: What should you check first in a music tool's terms?

choices.text: The color scheme of the app

questions.intro: MUSIC GENERATORS create songs, beats or background tracks from text descriptions. Before using generated music, check the RIGHTS. (1) The tool's TERMS: may you use it commercially, for example in a monetized video? Is credit required? Some free plans allow only personal use. (2) COPYRIGHT: in the United States, the Copyright Office's January 2025 report said that prompts alone do not make you the author of the output; your own lyrics, melodies or meaningful edits can be protected. (3) SIMILARITY: if a track sounds very like an existing song or imitates a specific artist's voice, avoid it. Keep a record of the tool, plan and date.

sections.skill: Compare music rights with borrowing a library book

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: What rules come with a library book?

choices.text: You can read it but not sell copies
You must read it in one day
You can do anything at all with it

questions.correct_answer: You can read it but not sell copies
questions.intro: A LIBRARY BOOK comes with rules: you can read it at home, but you cannot photocopy it and sell copies. Generated music also comes with rules, set by the tool's TERMS: a free plan may allow personal use only, while a paid plan may allow selling. And just as writing your name in a library book does not make you its author, typing a prompt does not by itself make you the author of the song, according to the US Copyright Office.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Reduce rights risks while the law develops

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: Are rights questions about generated music fully settled?

choices.text: No; they are still being argued
Yes, the same in every country

questions.correct_answer: No; they are still being argued
questions.intro: Rights questions are still being argued in courts and agencies, and answers differ by country, so this course does not settle them. Practical steps reduce risk: read the current terms, not old ones; keep proof of your plan when you generated the track; avoid prompts like "in the voice of" a named singer; and for school or public events, follow the venue's rules on music. Platforms may also remove or flag content whose music matches existing recordings.
